interest: For historians, this file offers an exceptional window into the immediate, chaotic transitional phase between wartime operations and postwar occupation, illustrating how archives were treated simultaneously as high-value military intelligence, legal instruments for disarmament and war crimes prosecution, and symbols of national sovereignty. It reveals the granular legal and geopolitical tensions of the early postwar order, notably the friction between U.S. insistence on physical custody versus host nations (such as Mexico and Colombia) asserting sovereign control, Soviet-Western rivalries emerging in peripheral diplomatic posts, and French anger over exclusion by the 'Big Four.' Additionally, the extensive inventories and interrogations derived from Berlin provide a remarkably detailed, primary-level record of German-Japanese military-industrial transfers and the disintegrating morale of Japanese personnel stranded in Europe at the close of the war.
overview: This file documents the worldwide diplomatic, military intelligence, and administrative efforts undertaken by the United States and Allied powers between July and October 1945 to locate, secure, impound, and exploit Japanese diplomatic, consular, and government records, properties, and technical intelligence in the immediate aftermath of World War II. The records encompass two central dimensions: extensive intelligence compilations—produced by G-2 USFET and the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey from captured Berlin embassy files and German industrial records—detailing German-Japanese wartime technical collaboration in synthetic fuels, aviation, armaments, and naval equipment; and intricate global diplomatic negotiations spanning Latin America, neutral Europe, and the Middle East to wrest Japanese archives and premises from protecting powers (notably Switzerland, Sweden, and Spain) while navigating host-country sovereignty and awaiting formal surrender directives from General Douglas MacArthur’s headquarters in Tokyo.
